I was thinking about this and hit upon a realization rooted in modern entertainment.

While the inability to think internally has probably always been around to some degree, I believe it's progressed at an exponential rate since the advent of modern cinema and television (probably the mid-1940's on). The trend likely began accelerating as the era of radio show entertainment ended and picked up sometime in the mid-80's to early-90's.

If you wanted to enjoy radio shows back in the day, at most you had static-filled sound effects to rely on for the sake of story progression, maybe a few distinctive voices crackling through. To get maximum enjoyment from the format, you had to be able to take in rich verbal descriptions and paint a mental picture for yourself to "see" the action taking place. This sort of neural activity has to be at least part-skill, lost without practice, perhaps even bred out over time across lower-quality bloodlines.

If we examine movies popular in the 80's and 90's, there are lots of moments where characters will simply stare off into the distance and we hear what they're thinking being narrated in voiceover. Similar to radio shows, this forces us (with little visual aid aside from maybe the actor's facial expressions) to independently make sense of the input, although in the case of movies the technique was more often used for comedic effect (and still is today).

As TV/movie technology progressed (and continues to do so even now), there became less of a need for audience interpretation as part of the story-telling experience. Multi-million dollar budgets allow directors to show us exactly what's happening with little or no wiggle room for speculation. Even reading books to children is no longer really a thing since so many parents now opt for interactive story apps on tablet devices and treat TV as a surrogate parent.

Stories have also became incredibly formulaic, with more abstract films and shows relegated to fringe audiences. I think all of this ultimately contributes to today's atrophied brain capacity and results in NPC-like behavior in which the input must come from an external source telling them what to think. Hell, some people may even start thinking in emojis (if they aren't already) since the culture of language is slowly reverting back to hieroglyphs.

Anyhow, that's just my take on it. I know it probably all seems obvious but maybe breaking this down further can help reveal more about this fascinating phenomenon. I haven't really been able to find any studies or info on the subject, but that may be because I'm not looking properly.
